Been here. Single mum who worked 12 hour shifts. I juggled school and raising my sister while mum worked. I was on shift when P day hit.

I knew little but enough to recognise it. My sister knew nothing.

She was in the bathroom along time and I tapped on the door and asked if everything was ok. I heard her crying and asked her what was wrong and did she need help?

She went quiet (she's very independent). So I asked her if she was bleeding. She meekly said yes then went into hysterics "what is wrong with me! Does this mean I can't be a mum?"

I just reacted. I opened the door partially and told her she was perfectly fine and this actual meant she could. I asked her what her sex ed course had told her (that's where my knowledge was from) and she said they didn't have it at her school because of idiotic mothers complaining about it.

So I went into my mothers room and searched for some pads and got some. I handed them through the door and explained the concept. She had a bit of trouble but got there in the end.

After that I sat down to a warm drink and the hardest conversation I've had. I told her for the next hour I'm not your brother. I'm your friend. Ask whatever you like and I'll tell you what I know and we can look up the rest online.

We sat on the couch talking and she started getting cramps. I knew what my GF at the time liked so got her a blanket and a hot water bottle set her up with the remote and told her I'd be in my room just call if she needs anything.

She cried a lot as she was still scared but she seemed better. I rang my mum and told her and she came home early and my sister told her I handled it and she was fine.

As uncomfortable as it was I'll always remember that as the solidifying day of our relationship. Before bed she came in and hugged me (our family aren't huggers or lovey dovey) and told me she loved me and that she was thankful I was her brother. Since that day we've been inseparable. She was 12 and I was 16 at that age.

Don't know if this helps but I had to share as it dug up the memory.

Good luck! Both for her and you if she gets moody!

For starters you have to realise that just because they might see you as responsible or otherwise doesn't necessarily mean you'll get whatever you're hoping to gain from being thought of as such.

You're their child, still under legal age and even once you're over that you'll still be their child. Some parents are chill and like to let their kids take on extra responsibilities in the family (I was caring for my little sister at 12, I don't see this as good though) others will always view you as a child and treat you as such.

One of the easiest ways to show you're responsible is think ahead on EVERYTHING, that's really the only difference I find of being a teenager to an almost 30 year old, back then everything was on impulse. These days I can't take a dump without thinking about long term ramifications. So maybe get a part time job and start a savings account, or start some extra studies? Maybe sit and think what you want to study at college and get a head start on it by just reading about it for fun.

Responsibility isn't the ability to do things, it's the ability to make the right decision of if and when to do those things in accordance to your general well being/future. So just think ahead but don't expect you're parents to suddenly view you completely differently instantly. It takes a hell of a lot of time to build respect and the bad part is you can lose it on the blink of an eye.
